content.thinking:
I’ve just executed a fairly involved test script (`/tmp/ns_test.js`) that spawns the NeonStrike server on port 3777, creates two mock clients, runs through a full join‑damage‑death‑score cycle, and then exits. The script’s stdout shows the server started (`NEONSTRIKE server running at http://localhost:3777`) and a series of JSON messages confirming that the server correctly handled player creation, joining, state updates, damage, death, and scoring. The test script itself does not explicitly terminate the server process; it relies on the spawned child process to exit when the script’s event loop finishes. However, I can’t be certain that the Node process has fully terminated – it might still be listening on the port, which would be a resource leak and could interfere with subsequent tests or deployments.

The next logical step is to clean up the temporary test script file I created, because it’s no longer needed and I don’t want stray files littering the archive. At the same time, I need to verify that the server process is indeed no longer listening on port 3777. The simplest way to do that is to issue an HTTP request to the root URL of the server and inspect the response. If the server is still running, `curl` will return a status code (e.g., 200) and a `Content-Type` header; if it has stopped, the connection will be refused and `curl` will produce no output (or an error, which I’ll suppress). I’ll use `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{content_type}\n'` to silently fetch the page, discard the body, and print just the status code and content type. Redirecting stderr to `/dev/null` ensures any connection‑refused errors don’t clutter the output.

Finally, I’ll append `echo done` so the command line gives me a clear marker that the cleanup sequence completed, making the output easy to parse later.

All of this can be done in a single Bash invocation, which keeps the session tidy and guarantees the steps run in order: first delete the temporary script, then probe the server, then signal completion.

Thus I’ll issue the Bash command:

`rm /tmp/ns_test.js; curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{content_type}\n' http://localhost:3777/ 2>/dev/null; echo done`

This satisfies both cleanup and verification requirements.

arguments.description: Clean up test script, confirm server stopped
